newsitem.title: USA: U.S. starts moving Kurds to Guam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. starts moving Kurds to Guam.

text.p: The United States began airlifting more than 2,000 former employees in northern Iraq from Turkey to the Pacific island of Guam on Monday to give them a new life in America far from the clutches of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

A total of 792 people, mainly Kurds, left the Turkish city of Diyarbakir for Guam aboard two chartered aircraft, State Department officials said. They said it was hoped to evacuate all 2,075 people on five flights by Thursday.

Most of the refugees worked as employees of U.S. aid programmes and the U.S.-led air operation patrolling a no-fly zone for Iraqi aircraft in northern Iraq. Some are reported to have been engaged in U.S. intelligence activities.

They had been holed up in small hotels and private homes waiting to escape since Iraqi troops entered the Western- protected Kurdish area to help the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) take the city of Arbil from a rival faction on Aug. 31.
That move, boosting Saddam's control of a region where he had been ineffective for the past five years, prompted U.S. cruise missile strikes on Iraq in early September.
Following U.S.-Turkish negotiations, the former U.S. employees and their household dependents crossed the mountainous border from Iraq into Turkey over the weekend.
"All of the local employees who worked with the United States in northern Iraq have made it from northern Iraq into Turkey. Every single one of them," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

Phyllis Oakley, Assistant Secretary of State for Population, Refugees and Migration, said the Kurds would start arriving on Tuesday at Anderson Air Force Base on Guam, a U.S. territory east of the Philippines, after a 14-hour flight from Turkey.
There they are expected to formally seek asylum and will be interviewed by eight to 10 officers of the Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS), Oakley told a briefing.
"Our expectation is, of course, that we will look very favourably upon this," Burns said.

"We have felt that we had an obligation to these people, since they stuck by us during the last five years, for us now to stick by them at a time when it was logical for us to conclude that Saddam Hussein and his security goons might inflict punishment or even worse upon them."

Oakley disclosed that even before Iraqi forces moved on Arbil, U.S. officials had looked at possible evacuation plans for U.S. employees because of rising tensions in northern Iraq. She gave no details.

The decision to move the Kurds to Guam enables them to be considered for what is called "parole" into the United States without preliminary decisions on visas and refugee status that would be necessary if they were processed overseas.

First reports were that the refugees might be kept up to three months in Turkey, but Burns said it had been decided to move them straight away because of the onset of winter and the plentiful supply of military housing on Guam.

Neither Burns nor Oakley admitted to any pressure from the Turkish government to move the Kurds out immediately. Oakley said the Turkish authorities had been "really wonderful" and "very cooperative" in the matter.

Turkey is known to have been concerned about possible infiltration by guerrillas of the Kurdish Workers' Party (PKK), which is waging an armed separatist struggle against the Turkish government and has bases in northern Iraq.
Burns and Oakley said U.S. officials had identified the refugees and were confident there were no PKK guerrillas among them.

Oakley said the cost of the evacuation would run into millions of dollars, but she declined to give a precise estimate. She said the cost would be split between the State Department, the Defence Department and the INS.
